A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same temporal label-noise framework and estimation methods despite the changed title and terminology. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic and real-dataset experiments, noise-estimation results, ablations, and an Extrasensory case study in Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark and multiclass results, plus stress-detection experiments comparing predictions and estimated noise against physiological labels.

M1.justification: v2 removes the backward sequence loss as a proposed training alternative, narrowing the methodology to forward correction. The three retained estimators match across renaming: TENOR becomes Continuous, VolMinTime becomes Discontinuous, and AnchorTime becomes Plug-In; their retained architecture and implementation descriptions do not establish new procedures.

E1.justification: v1's Extrasensory sleep-transition study involving 60 users disappears, while v2 introduces stress detection for 289 healthcare workers with self-reported and physiological labels. The four principal real datasets are renamed rather than replaced, and synthetic and multiclass coverage remains in the appendices.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparator set remains equivalent after renaming. However, v2 removes the backward-loss comparator from Figure 5 and drops the supplementary comparisons involving VolMinTime's alternative penalties and augmented-Lagrangian variant.

E3.justification: The real-noise evaluation changes substantially: v1 centers Extrasensory windows on sleep transitions and inspects inferred noise without clean labels; v2 evaluates stress predictions and noise estimates against physiological labels and reports '10-CV' estimates. The retained semi-synthetic experiments keep the 80/20 split, preprocessing, model architectures, and 150-epoch training budget.

E4.justification: v2 removes the forward-versus-backward analysis, penalty/optimization controls, class-dependent versus class-independent periodic-noise comparison, and extensive binary noise-level sweeps from v1 Appendix E. It adds the stress case study and four-method ablation in Section 6. The forward-loss misspecification analysis and multiclass sweeps remain.

E5.justification: Retained experiments continue reporting means and standard deviations over ten runs. The new stress study reports mean '10-CV' estimates with standard deviations, adding a cross-validation reporting procedure; the PDFs do not specify its fold construction or establish increased repetition of existing experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds stress results, including 25.5 ± 1.7% test error for Continuous versus 31.1 ± 4.3% for Ignore, and removes numerous appendix results. Some retained table entries change beyond accuracy/error conversion: har70 VolMinTime's 82.0% accuracy becomes senior Discontinuous's 13.6% error. Approximation-error values also change scale without sufficient explanation to infer same-setting gains.

T1.justification: v2 deletes the backward-loss definition, equivalence theorem, and supporting lemmas and proofs from v1 Section 2.2 and Appendix A. The forward-loss guarantee and derivation remain as Proposition 1. Renaming the Markov Assumption to Future Independence retains its mathematical statement.

C1.justification: The advertised loss contribution narrows from two losses to one, and the explicit claim that TENOR is the first temporal-noise estimator becomes a contribution framed as a suite of methods. The central claims about formalizing temporal noise and outperforming static approaches remain; the conclusion additionally emphasizes stress-detection validation.

C2.justification: v2 adds a stationarity limitation and interprets stress results through noise estimation, training error, and generalization. It removes the backward-loss instability explanation and v1's discussion of assumption verification and missing finite-sample guarantees. The shared-noise-function limitation remains, while the shortage of paired clean/noisy labels becomes an explicit limitation.

D1.justification: Extrasensory window-construction details are replaced by stress-study dimensions and label descriptions, while shared training hyperparameters, architectures, and the code link remain. The explicit discontinuous log-determinant objective is omitted. v2 also introduces inconsistent moving feature counts: 14 in Tables 2–3 versus 9 in Appendix Table 6.

R1.justification: v2 adds stress and digital-health references, non-stationary learning work by Kuznetsov and Mohri, and newer label-noise citations. It removes Extrasensory and several memorization and sample-selection references. The central positioning against static noise correction and existing time-series noise identification remains.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, methodology, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes a separate numbered section, methods are reorganized around formulation and estimation, terminology changes throughout, and the appendices are consolidated and reordered. The title, affiliations, and acknowledgements also change.

P2.justification: The main text switches from two columns to one, benchmark tables are transposed and reorganized, and Figures 1–2 are redesigned. Stress receives a new figure and table, a notation table is introduced, and numerous appendix plots disappear. Retained multiclass figures are relabeled and relocated.

improvement.justification: Section 6 strengthens practical validation: v1's Extrasensory study could only inspect inferred noise, whereas v2 measures predictive and estimation errors against physiological labels designated as clean. Clearer organization and the stationarity qualification also help. The net gain is limited by removal of optimization controls and binary robustness results, insufficient detail on stress-label construction, and inconsistent benchmark documentation.
